title: The K-th Number in Dictionary Order
statement:
Write the numbers `1, 2, ..., n` as texts and sort them in **dictionary order** (compare character by character; a shorter text that is the start of a longer one comes first). For `n = 13` the order is `1, 10, 11, 12, 13, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9`.

Return the `k`-th number in this order (counting from `1`).

hints.nudge: Picture all the numbers as a tree: 1 has the children 10 to 19, 10 has the children 100 to 109, and so on, and the dictionary order is the order in which a depth-first walk visits them. How many numbers are in the subtree of a given number?
hints.pattern: Walk down the tree without visiting every number: for the current prefix count how many numbers (up to n) start with it; if the k-th is not inside, skip the whole subtree and go to the next prefix; otherwise go one level deeper.
hints.walkthrough: Sorting the texts of all numbers is O(n log n) and impossible for n = 10^9. Use the tree view: the children of a prefix p are 10p, 10p + 1, ..., 10p + 9, and the numbers in the subtree of p are found level by level as the ranges [p, p], [10p, 10p + 9], [100p, 100p + 99], ..., each cut at n. Their total is the subtree size. Start at 1 and use up k - 1 steps: if the whole subtree of the current prefix is not larger than the remaining steps, jump to the next sibling (prefix + 1) and subtract the subtree size; otherwise the answer is inside it: step to the first child (prefix * 10) and use one step. Each decision costs O(log n) and there are O(log n) levels, so O(log^2 n) overall. The ranges can reach 10^10, so use 64-bit numbers.
